I appear in the sky after rain, painted in a curved band of many colours, but no matter how far you walk, you can never reach me. What am I?
I am a delicate trap spun from silk thread to catch flies, and no human hand can weave me quite as well. What am I?
I carry my house on my back wherever I go, and I leave a shiny trail of slime behind me. What am I?
In Yoruba and Igbo folktales I am the clever, greedy animal who often outsmarts bigger animals, and I carry a hard shell on my back. What am I?
I can change the colour of my skin to match my surroundings, move very slowly, and my two eyes can look in two different directions at once. What am I?
I am a colourful bird kept as a pet, and I can copy the words that humans say to me. What am I?
I am a bird with a bald head who circles high in the sky, waiting for animals to die so I can feed on them. What am I?
I am tiny and I buzz near your ear at night, and after I bite you, your skin itches for days. What am I?
I scurry away into the cracks the moment the kitchen light comes on, and I can survive almost anywhere in a house. What am I?
I am made from grated, fermented cassava, then fried into small crunchy yellow grains that Nigerians soak in cold water or eat as eba. What am I?
I am spicy grilled meat on a stick, coated in a peanut-based spice mix, and sold by roadside vendors at night. What am I?
I am a pot of rice cooked in a rich tomato and pepper sauce, and Nigerians and Ghanaians love to argue about who cooks me best. What am I?
I look like a big banana, but I must be cooked before eating, and I am often fried into golden slices called dodo. What am I?
I am a fizzy white drink tapped straight from the top of a palm tree, and I turn sour the longer I am left standing. What am I?
I am a deep red drink made by boiling dried hibiscus leaves, then sweetened and served cold. What am I?
In Igbo tradition it is said 'he who brings me brings life' before I am broken into pieces and shared among visitors to welcome them. What am I?
I am a long piece of colourful cloth that Nigerian women tie around their waist as part of traditional dress. What am I?
I am an elaborately tied head wrap worn standing tall and stiff by Nigerian women, especially at weddings. What am I?
I am a wide, flowing gown with big sleeves worn by Nigerian men on special occasions, usually over a smaller shirt called a buba. What am I?
I am a deep hole dug into the ground to reach water, and you lower a bucket tied to a rope into me. What am I?
I have one wheel and two handles, and builders push me around filled with sand or cement. What am I?
I am a long, sharp blade that Nigerian farmers swing to clear bush and cut through tall grass. What am I?
I have a flat blade fixed to a wooden handle, and farmers use me to turn and loosen soil before planting, not to cut anything. What am I?
I must be broken before I can be of any use, and inside me you will often find a golden yolk. What am I?
A small flame appears the moment you click my button, and I am small enough to fit in your pocket. What am I?
I have many pages, one for each day of the year, and you write your private thoughts or plans inside me. What am I?
I am printed fresh every morning, full of yesterday's news, and by evening I am already old and thrown away. What am I?
I have eight legs and I spin silk to trap my prey, but I am not an insect at all. What am I?

I start life crawling as a caterpillar, sleep inside a cocoon, then wake with colourful wings. I am usually active in daylight, resting with my wings folded upright, unlike my night-loving cousin. What am I?
I am a small crawling creature with many legs, and very soon I will transform completely while resting inside a cocoon. What am I?
I fly from flower to flower collecting nectar, live in a hive with a queen, and can sting a person only once before I die. What am I?
I am tiny, but I march in long visible lines carrying crumbs back to my underground colony, which has a queen. What am I?
I hop instead of walk and croak at night near ponds. My skin is smooth and moist, unlike my bumpy, dry-skinned cousin. What am I?
I live in water with a long tail but no legs yet, and one day I will grow up into a frog. What am I?
I store fat in the hump on my back, and I can travel many days across the desert without drinking water. What am I?
I am known for being stubborn, I have long ears, and I carry heavy loads on farms. I am a purebred animal, not a mix between a horse and another animal like my hybrid cousin. What am I?
I have the longest neck of any land animal, spotted patches on my skin, and I eat leaves from the tops of trees. What am I?
I look like a horse, but I am covered in black and white stripes, and no two of us share exactly the same pattern. What am I?
I am a bird famous for the male's huge, colourful tail that opens like a fan to attract a mate. What am I?
I am the largest bird in the world, but I cannot fly — instead I run very fast on two long legs. What am I?
I am a tall bird that often stands on one leg in shallow water, easy to spot because my feathers are bright pink. What am I?
I walk sideways on the beach, I have two big pincer claws, and I carry my skeleton on the outside of my body. What am I?
I have numbers marked along my body, and doctors and weather reporters use me to tell how hot or cold something is. What am I?
Step on me at the clinic, and I will tell you your weight in kilograms. What am I?
I am a long, flexible strip marked with numbers, rolled up inside a small case, used by tailors and builders to measure length. What am I?
I have a needle that always points north, helping travellers and sailors find their direction. What am I?
I can pull iron and steel objects toward me without ever touching them first. What am I?
I am a long tube fitted with lenses that makes faraway stars and planets look close, letting astronomers study the night sky. What am I?
I make tiny things too small for the eye to see look huge, and scientists use me in the lab to study germs. What am I?
I am a round piece of curved glass with a handle, and holding me over small print makes the letters look much bigger. What am I?
I sit on your nose and rest on your ears, helping people see clearly who cannot see well on their own. What am I?
I have sleeves and buttons down the front, and I am worn over your clothes to keep you dry in the rain, unlike the sleeveless cover you simply pull over your head. What am I?
I have a spout and a handle, and I whistle loudly once the water inside me starts to boil. What am I?
I keep hot food or drinks hot for hours, or cold drinks cold, all without using any electricity. What am I?
I use electricity to keep food and drinks cold, and behind my door you find fresh vegetables and bottled drinks, not ice blocks. What am I?
I keep things frozen completely solid, turning water into hard blocks of ice inside me. What am I?
I have spinning blades at the bottom of a jug, and I turn fruit into smoothies or tomatoes into a smooth puree. What am I?
I have spinning blades that push air around the room to cool you down, but I never actually change the temperature of the air itself. What am I?
I am fixed to a wall or window, and unlike my simpler cousin that just blows air around, I truly cool the air inside the room. What am I?
I have a screen that shows moving pictures and sound, and Nigerian families gather around me to watch Nollywood movies and the evening news. What am I?
I have no screen, only sound, and I carry music and news through the air into homes and cars. What am I?
I fit in your pocket, and with me you can call, text, and browse the internet all at once. What am I?
I plug straight into the wall socket, and I feed power into your phone's battery until it is full again. What am I?
I have a USB port, and I must be charged myself first before I can share my stored power to charge your phone away from any wall socket. What am I?
I run on batteries, and pressing my switch sends a bright beam of light stabbing into the darkness. What am I?
I burn kerosene inside a glass case to give light, and I have a wick that must be trimmed and lit with a match. What am I?
I hang on the outside of a door or gate, and only the correct key can open my shackle. What am I?
I am made of connected metal links, and I can be used to lock a gate or pull a heavy object. What am I?
I am made of twisted fibres, and people use me to tie things together or to climb up and down. What am I?
I have two long sides with many steps between them, and unlike the fixed steps built inside a house, you can carry me from place to place and lean me against a wall. What am I?
I have a handle and an open top, and you fill me with water at the well or tap to carry it home. What am I?
I am a plastic or metal container with a narrow capped neck, often yellow, used to carry fuel or water long distances. What am I?
I am a wide, shallow bowl used for washing clothes and plates, or bathing a baby. What am I?
I am a thin strand that passes through the eye of a needle, and I hold pieces of cloth together once they are sewn. What am I?
I am a small disc with holes, sewn onto clothes, and I fit through a hole to keep a shirt closed. What am I?
I have two rows of teeth that lock together when you pull my little tab up, and come apart when you pull it down. What am I?
I am a long thin string that you tie in a bow to keep your shoe snug on your foot. What am I?
I am soft and filled with foam or feathers, and you rest your head on me when you go to sleep at night. What am I?
I am a large piece of soft cloth that you pull over your whole body at night to keep warm. What am I?
I am thick and soft, resting on top of a bed frame, and you lie your whole body on me to sleep. What am I?
I lie flat on the floor, and people wipe their feet on me before entering a house, or kneel on me to pray. What am I?
I hang beside a window, and I can be drawn across the glass to block out sunlight or give privacy. What am I?
I am a flat, heavy stone, and before blenders existed, Nigerian grandmothers rubbed pepper and tomatoes against my flat surface to make a smooth paste. What am I?
In Yoruba culture, I am an hourglass-shaped drum held under the arm; squeezing my cords while I'm struck changes my pitch so I can 'talk' like a human voice. What am I?
Long before newspapers and radio reached the village, I walked the streets at dawn beating a metal gong and shouting announcements from the chief. What am I?
I am a small cube wrapped in foil, and Nigerian cooks crumble me into soup or stew to make it taste richer, though I add no visible ingredient of my own besides flavour. What am I?
Between November and February, I blow dusty, dry wind down from the Sahara across Nigeria, cracking lips and skin, and hiding the sun behind a hazy veil. What am I?
In a Nigerian shop, when the network is good, you tap or swipe your card on me and I print a small paper slip proving you've paid, all without you touching cash. What am I?
The moment money enters or leaves your account, I arrive on your phone as a short text message telling you the amount and your new balance. What am I?
I am a small card with a silver panel; scratch it off to reveal a hidden number, and typing that number into your phone gives you credit to call or browse. What am I?
I am a tiny chip that lives inside your phone, storing your phone number; without me, your phone cannot make calls on any network. What am I?
I have several holes in a row and one plug at my tail; plugging me into a single wall socket lets several appliances share that one source of power. What am I?
I am a thin green spiral that you light at one end; I do not burn fast like a candle, but smoulder slowly all night, filling the room with smoke that drives mosquitoes away. What am I?
I have a smooth, heavy metal base that gets very hot, and running me over crumpled clothes leaves them smooth and neat. What am I?
I have a hook at the top and two sloping arms below; you drape a shirt over me inside a wardrobe so it keeps its shape instead of wrinkling in a pile. What am I?
Long before naira notes and coins, Nigerian traders exchanged small white shells gathered from the sea to buy and sell in the market. What were these shells called?
Only a king may wear me: a tall, beaded crown, often with a fringe of beads hanging in front of the face, used in Yoruba royal tradition. What am I?
I run along the edge of a roof, catching rainwater and channelling it down a pipe so it doesn't pour directly onto people below. What am I?
I stand at road junctions with three colours stacked one above another; red tells cars to stop, and green tells them to go. What am I?
I am a series of thick white stripes painted across a road, showing pedestrians exactly where it's safest to walk across. What am I?
I am a raised ridge built across a road; I force even fast drivers to slow down as their car bumps over me. What am I?
I am a hole that forms in the middle of a tarred road after heavy rain, and drivers swerve around me to protect their tyres. What am I?
I am a flat blue-black panel fixed on a rooftop; I quietly turn sunlight into electricity without burning any fuel. What am I?

I store electricity in a battery while the light is on, then switch on automatically and silently to power your fan and bulbs the moment NEPA takes the light, unlike my noisier, fuel-drinking cousin. What am I?
I sit between the wall socket and your television or fridge, correcting the unsteady voltage from the national grid so your appliances are not damaged by sudden surges. What am I?
I am a wide, flat metal pan without a handle, and Nigerian labourers balance me on their heads to carry sand, gravel, or cement at a building site. What am I?
Slice me and I release a slippery, stretchy juice that makes the soup I'm cooked in slide easily off a ball of eba. What am I?
I am ground from dried melon seeds into a coarse powder, then cooked into a thick, nutty soup that Nigerians eat with pounded yam or fufu. What am I?
I come from the seed of a wild 'bush mango' fruit, dried and ground into powder; once cooked, I make soup extremely thick and 'drawy', stretching in long strings when scooped. What am I?

I am a soup made by boiling and pounding the fruit of the palm tree to extract a reddish-orange sauce, popular among the Niger Delta and Edo people, quite different from the clear liquid tapped from that same tree's trunk. What am I?
I am a light, watery, fiery soup made with lots of pepper and spices, often served with goat meat or fish, and Nigerians eat me to 'sweat out' a cold or as a starter at parties. What am I?
I am made from a smooth paste of peeled beans blended with pepper and onions, then steamed wrapped in leaves or a tin until I set firm, without ever touching hot oil. What am I?
I am made from the same blended bean paste as my steamed cousin, but instead I am scooped straight into hot oil and deep-fried until my outside turns crisp and golden-brown. What am I?

I am made from a soft, sweet dough of flour, sugar and yeast, deep-fried into round golden balls that are fluffy and airy inside, quite different from my crunchy, diamond-cut cousin sold in a small transparent bag. What am I?
I am a sweet, crunchy snack cut into small diamond or cube shapes from a stiff dough, then fried until hard and golden, often packed in a bag for a party or long journey. What am I?
I am thin sheets of beef, coated in a spicy peanut paste, then sun-dried until I become tough and chewy like a cracker; I am often called the 'beef jerky' of Northern Nigeria. What am I?
I am chopped, grilled goat meat tossed in hot pepper and onions, and Nigerians love to eat me as a peppery side dish at parties, usually with a cold drink. What am I?
I am a whole goat head, cooked and served in a thick spicy sauce with the skin still on, a prized delicacy at many Igbo celebrations. What am I?
I am cow foot cooked slowly in a spicy palm oil and potash sauce, usually served hot in a wooden mortar-shaped bowl as a favourite side dish at Nigerian parties. What am I?
I am a smooth, cream-coloured swallow made from processed wheat, cooked with hot water and stirred into a soft, stretchy dough eaten with soup. What am I?
I am a swallow made from dried, ground yam flour, giving me a distinctive dark brown colour unlike any of my other swallow cousins. What am I?
I am a soft swallow made by cooking rice or guinea corn until it forms a smooth mash, popular in Northern Nigeria and often eaten with miyan kuka or other soups. What am I?
I am a Northern Nigerian drink made of small balls of cooked millet mixed into fermented cow's milk, giving a slightly sour, refreshing taste. What am I?
Roadside vendors roast me whole over open coals until my skin turns black and my inside softens, then serve me hot beside grilled fish or groundnuts. What am I?
I am thin, hard, deep-fried plantain chips, usually made from unripe plantain sliced thin, salted, and crunched loudly between the teeth. What am I?
I am the largest land animal alive, with two long curved tusks and a trunk that I use like a built-in hose, hand, and snorkel all in one. What am I?
I spend most of the day submerged in African rivers to keep my huge grey body cool, and despite my slow, clumsy look on land, I am one of the most dangerous animals to encounter. What am I?
I have thick, armour-like grey skin and one or two horns growing from my snout, and poachers hunt me illegally just for those horns. What am I?

I lie completely still at the water's edge in African rivers, looking like a floating log, until an unsuspecting animal comes close enough for my powerful jaws to snap shut; unlike my similar-looking cousin found mainly in the Americas, I roam free across Nigeria's waterways. What am I?
I am covered from head to tail in hard, overlapping scales made of keratin, and when threatened I curl into a tight, armoured ball instead of fighting back. What am I?
I share a huge amount of DNA with humans, I live in social troops across African forests, and I am famous for poking sticks into mounds to 'fish' out termites to eat. What am I?
I am the largest living primate, with males developing a patch of silver-grey fur on their backs as they mature, and I mostly eat leaves and stems rather than meat. What am I?
I can turn my head almost all the way around, I hunt silently at night thanks to soft-edged feathers, and my hooting call makes many people uneasy after dark. What am I?
I am the only mammal that can truly fly, I sleep hanging upside down in caves or under roofs by day, and I find my way in total darkness by bouncing sound off objects around me. What am I?
My back is covered in hundreds of short, sharp spines, and when danger comes near, I simply roll myself into a tight, prickly ball. What am I?
I have eight flexible arms lined with suckers, three hearts pumping blue blood, a soft round body with no fins, and I can squirt a cloud of ink to vanish from predators. What am I?
I am made almost entirely of water, I have no brain, no heart, and no bones, yet my trailing tentacles can deliver a painful sting. What am I?
Unlike almost every other animal, it is the male of my species who becomes pregnant and gives birth, carrying the eggs in a special pouch on his belly. What am I?
I carry my baby in a pouch on my belly, I use my powerful hind legs to hop rather than walk, and I am found wild only in Australia. What am I?
I sleep up to 20 hours a day in the branches of eucalyptus trees, and the leaves I eat are so low in nutrients and mildly toxic that they force me to move very slowly. What am I?
I move so slowly that algae grows in my fur, turning me faintly green, and I spend almost my entire life hanging upside down from tree branches in Central and South America. What am I?
I have a duck-like bill, webbed feet, and lay eggs like a bird, yet I am covered in fur and nurse my young with milk like a mammal. What am I?
Two words sound exactly the same when spoken aloud: one means the number after seven, and the other is a past-tense word meaning consumed food. Which spelling means the number?
I am a device that uses radio waves to detect the speed and location of distant objects like aircraft or speeding cars, and my own name reads identically backwards. What am I?
Say me aloud and I could mean the colourful bloom in a garden, or the fine white powder ground from wheat that bakers use for bread. Which spelling means the baking powder?
I am an insect with strong back legs built for jumping, and my English name is formed by joining a patch of green lawn with the action of leaping. What am I?

I am a fast-flying insect with two pairs of shimmering wings and a long, slender body, and my English name pairs a mythical fire-breathing creature with the act of flying, even though I am neither dangerous nor related to that creature. What am I?
I am a small, round beetle, usually red or orange with black spots, and my common English name oddly includes the word for a female human, even though I am an insect. What am I?
I am a small beetle that lights up my own body in the dark using a chemical reaction, flashing on summer nights to attract a mate. What am I?
I have no eyes, no legs, and no lungs, yet by tunnelling endlessly through soil I keep it loose and fertile for farmers. What am I?
I am a short sentence, famous among typists and typographers, that uses every single letter of the English alphabet at least once, and I mention a quick fox and a lazy dog. What sentence am I?
questions.answer: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog

questions.question: I am a common English word of nine letters, yet I contain only a single vowel. What word am I?
I am an English verb that can mean either to remove fine particles from a surface, or to sprinkle fine particles onto it — two opposite actions hiding in one single word. What word am I?
I am a word that can mean either to officially approve and permit something, or to penalise and punish it — two opposite meanings packed into one word. What word am I?
I am a six-letter word meaning 'to pay close attention with your ears'; rearrange all my letters and I become a word meaning 'making no sound at all'. What word am I (the attentive one)?

I am a nine-letter word for a large shared sleeping room, often found in a hostel or boarding school. Every one of my letters can be rearranged to spell out a cheeky two-word description of an untidy room. What word am I?
I am the only number, when spelled out in English, whose letters appear in strict alphabetical order from first to last. What number am I?
Spelled out in English, my letters run in exact descending alphabetical order — and no other number's name does this. Which small number am I?
The phrase 'ELEVEN PLUS TWO' is a rearrangement of the exact same letters as another arithmetic phrase that also equals thirteen. What is that other phrase?
I run along a road with sharp twisted points spaced along my length, coiled or straight, used to stop people or animals from crossing a boundary. What am I?
I flick on automatically at dusk and switch off at dawn, using a light sensor rather than a manual switch, to keep a compound lit through the night. What am I?
A phone dealer in Computer Village buys a phone for 85,000 naira and sells it at a 20% profit. What is the selling price?
Ngozi is currently three times as old as her younger brother Chuka. In 8 years, she will only be twice his age. How old is Chuka right now?
A cooperative in Enugu lends a trader 20,000 naira at a simple interest rate of 10% per year. How much will the trader owe in total after 2 years?
Tolu can weed a farm alone in 6 hours. His sister Bisi can weed the same farm alone in 3 hours. Working together at their own steady paces, how many hours will it take them to weed the farm?
A tailor mixes red and white beads in the ratio 3:5 to make a necklace of 40 beads. How many red beads are used?
A danfo bus travels from Ojota to Berger, a distance of 60 kilometres, at a steady speed of 40 kilometres per hour. How many minutes does the journey take?
Out of 80 students in a Lagos classroom, 65% passed their mathematics exam. How many students failed?
I am a two-digit number. My digits add up to 9. If you reverse my digits, the new number is 27 more than me. What number am I?
I am a two-digit number. The sum of my digits is 11. If you reverse my digits, you get a number 45 more than me. What number am I?
Three consecutive whole numbers add up to 72. What is the largest of the three?
The sum of two numbers is 50 and their difference is 12. What is the larger number?
A farmer has both chickens and goats. Together they have 35 heads and 94 legs. How many goats does he have?
A clock strikes 6 o'clock in exactly 5 seconds, counting from the first chime to the last. If the pauses between chimes are equal, how many seconds will the same clock take to strike 12 o'clock?
A tap can fill a tank in 4 hours. A leak in the same tank can empty a full tank in 12 hours. If the tap is opened while the leak is also open, how long will it take to fill the empty tank?
A train 150 metres long is moving at 54 km/h. How many seconds does it take to completely cross a stationary pole?
A train 200 metres long moving at 72 km/h crosses a bridge in 30 seconds. How long is the bridge?
A boat travels downstream at 20 km/h and upstream at 12 km/h. What is the speed of the river current?
In 5 years, Efe will be twice as old as she was 5 years ago. How old is Efe now?
The combined age of a father and his son is 66 years. Six years ago, the father was 5 times as old as the son. How old is the son now?

A shopkeeper mixes 20 litres of palm oil worth 800 naira per litre with some litres of a cheaper oil worth 500 naira per litre, to get a mixture worth 650 naira per litre. How many litres of the cheaper oil did she use?
What is the next number in this sequence: 2, 3, 5, 9, 17, 33, ___?
What is the next number in this sequence: 1, 4, 9, 18, 35, ___?
What is the next number in this sequence: 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, ___?
What is the next number in this sequence: 100, 90, 81, 73, 66, ___?
Using A=1, B=2, C=3 ... Z=26, what is the letter-sum value of the word 'NAIJA'?
Chidi is twice as old as Ike. Five years ago, Chidi was three times as old as Ike was then. How old is Ike now?
Two okada riders start 90 km apart and ride towards each other, one at 30 km/h and the other at 20 km/h. After how many hours will they meet?
A cyclist leaves Lagos at 8 km/h. Two hours later, a second cyclist leaves the same point chasing at 12 km/h. How many hours after the second cyclist starts will she catch up to the first?
A shop increases the price of a shirt by 20%, then later offers a 20% discount off that new price. Compared to the original price, by what percentage is the final price lower?
10,000 naira is invested at 10% compound interest per year. What is the total amount after 2 years?
You have 8 identical-looking gold coins, but one is fake and slightly lighter than the rest. Using a balance scale, what is the minimum number of weighings needed to guarantee finding the fake coin?
Four friends sit in a row of four seats. Ada is not at either end. Bayo sits immediately to the left of Chika. Dapo sits at the far right. Who sits at the far left?

Five books are stacked in a pile. Maths sits directly on top of Biology. Physics is above Chemistry but below Maths. English is at the very bottom. Listing from top to bottom, what is the exact order of all five books?
In a class of 50 students, 30 study French, 25 study Yoruba, and 10 study both languages. How many students study neither language?
In a market survey of 100 traders, 60 sell foodstuff, 45 sell clothes, and 20 sell both. How many traders sell only foodstuff?
A number, when divided by 5, leaves remainder 3, and when divided by 7, leaves remainder 4. What is the smallest positive number that satisfies both conditions?
A ladder 10 metres long leans against a vertical wall, with its foot 6 metres from the base of the wall. How high up the wall does the ladder reach?
A rectangular farm is 3 times as long as it is wide, and its area is 300 square metres. What is its width?

Two workers, Emeka and Femi, can finish a job together in 6 days. Emeka alone can finish it in 15 days. If Emeka works alone for 3 days and then Femi joins him, how many more days will it take them together to finish the remaining work?
In the classic puzzle SEND + MORE = MONEY, where each letter stands for a unique digit, what digit does the letter M represent?
What is the longest common English word that can be typed using only the left hand on a standard QWERTY keyboard?
What is the longest English word that can be typed using only the letters found on the top row of a QWERTY keyboard?
Spell the word for feeling under pressure or strain backwards, and you get the name of a sweet course eaten at the end of a meal. What is the sweet course?
What do the words 'listen', 'silent', and 'enlist' have in common with each other?
questions.answer: They are anagrams of each other (made from the same six letters)

questions.question: If you spell out numbers in English starting from 'one', what is the first number, in both digits and words, whose spelling contains the letter 'A'?
Repeatedly add together the digits of the number 9875 until only a single digit remains. What is that digit?
What is the binary number 101101 when converted to decimal (base 10)?
What year, written in Roman numerals, is MCMXCIX?
Write the number 2024 in Roman numerals.

A rope ladder hangs over the side of a ship, with its bottom rung touching the water. The rungs are spaced 25 cm apart, and 10 rungs are above the water. If the tide rises 25 cm every hour for 3 hours, how many rungs will be above the water afterwards?
How many months of the year have at least 28 days?
If a plane crashes exactly on the border between two countries, in which country do they bury the survivors?
A snail at the bottom of a 10-metre well climbs up 3 metres every day but slips back 2 metres every night. On which day does it finally climb out of the well?
I am a horned animal, ritually slaughtered by Muslims during Eid-el-Kabir (Sallah), and my traditional name is distinct from a goat, even though we look similar. What am I?

I am a Nigerian musical instrument made from a large hollowed gourd covered with a net of beads or cowries; shaking and hitting me against the hand produces a rattling, rhythmic sound, common in Yoruba and Fuji music. What am I?
I was a large wooden-bodied bus that once roared through Lagos streets before newer buses replaced me, infamous for my rough rides and the nickname 'moving mortuary'. What am I?
12 labourers can build a wall in 8 days. How many labourers are needed to build the same wall in 6 days, assuming all labourers work at the same steady rate?
Pipe A fills a tank in 5 hours. Pipe B fills the same tank in 10 hours. If both pipes are opened together, how many hours will it take to fill the tank?
A car travels from Ibadan to Lagos at 60 km/h and returns the same route at 40 km/h. What is the average speed for the entire round trip?
What is the next number in this sequence: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, ___?
What is the next number in this sequence: 4, 7, 12, 19, 28, ___?
What is the next number in this sequence: 1, 2, 6, 24, 120, ___?
A father is currently 4 times as old as his son Tunde. In 8 years, the father will be 3 times as old as Tunde. How old is Tunde now?
The sum of the ages of three siblings is 45. The eldest is twice as old as the youngest, and the middle sibling is 5 years older than the youngest. How old is the youngest sibling?
A bag contains 4 red balls and 6 blue balls. If one ball is drawn at random, what is the probability, expressed as a fraction in lowest terms, that it is red?

A basket has 3 ripe mangoes and 2 unripe mangoes. If two mangoes are picked at random one after another without replacement, what is the probability that both are ripe? Express as a fraction in lowest terms.
